lessons.title: Variables

answers: 5 and 6 are different types
value is immutable without mut
Numbers cannot be reassigned
writing.exampleCaption: Shadowing makes a new binding; mut changes an existing one.
writing.exampleCode:
let total = 10;        // immutable
let total = total + 5; // shadowed
let mut counter = 0;   // mutable
counter += 1;
writing.explanation: Rust makes state changes visible in the code with mut, so a reader never has to guess whether something moves under them. Shadowing is a different tool: it creates a brand new binding with the same name, which may even have a different type, leaving the original untouched.
writing.feedback: Add mut, or shadow with a second let if a new binding is what you meant.
writing.practiceCode:
let value = 5;
value = 6;
writing.question: Why is the reassignment rejected?
writing.rule: mut permits mutation; shadowing replaces the binding entirely.
writing.success: It compiles with no unused-mutation warning.
writing.summary: Bindings are immutable unless you opt in.

writing.exampleCaption: Position for a tuple, index for an array.

writing.exampleCaption: Say what should happen at the boundary instead of hoping.
writing.explanation: There is no implicit numeric promotion: adding a u8 to a u32 is a compile error until you convert. lessons.title: Ranges

writing.exampleCaption: The two ranges have different upper-bound rules.
writing.explanation: The range 0..3 contains 0, 1, and 2; its upper bound is excluded. The inclusive form 1..=3 also contains 3. Half-open ranges fit indexing because a length can be used directly as the excluded end. Inclusive ranges are useful when both endpoints belong to the domain.
writing.feedback: The upper bound of .. is excluded, so 5 is not part of the range.
writing.practiceCode: let values: Vec<_> = (2..5).collect();
writing.question: Which values are collected?
writing.rule: a..b excludes b; a..=b includes b.
writing.success: The output has no missing or accidental extra endpoint.
writing.summary: Range syntax makes boundaries visible instead of hiding an off-by-one rule.

writing.exampleCaption: The move is what makes a double free impossible.
writing.explanation: Moves transfer that responsibility to a new binding and make the old one unusable. Copy types duplicate instead of moving, and Drop runs the moment the owner leaves scope — which is how Rust frees memory with no garbage collector and no possibility of a double free. When you genuinely need two usable values, clone() makes a second one that owns its own data.
writing.feedback: Cloning creates a second owned String rather than moving the first.
writing.question: What is the smallest fix that keeps both usable?
writing.rule: One value, one owner; a move ends the previous binding.
writing.success: You can explain why no double free is possible.
writing.summary: Ownership gives every value one clear cleanup responsibility.
